summary: Defines the go: URI scheme for use with the Common Name Resolution Protocol. It lays out the scheme's parts and how they are used to find the transports for a CNRP service. Some parts look like those in other URI schemes but behave differently.

plainLanguage.summary: A web address starts with a word like http. This document defines a new starting word, go, for links that say go find this by its common name.

subtitle: A compact URI format for pointing at a common-name lookup, or at one record on one server.

tldr.problem: A Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP) query is written in XML, and putting a complex XML query into a URI would quickly exceed URI length limits.
tldr.mechanism: The go: scheme defines a simplified query syntax, a subset of what the XML allows, made of an optional server, a common name and optional attribute=value pairs, or just an ID.
tldr.outcome: Clients get a short, linkable form for a CNRP query. The RFC warns that an ID-only URI hides which common name it refers to.

today: RFC 3368 is a Proposed Standard from August 2002. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Goals of the go: Scheme
sections.content:
The go: URI scheme is made for the Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP, RFC 3367). It has two goals: to identify a specific common-name record at a specific server, and to identify a possibly dynamic query or entry point into the query process.

Because CNRP requires the ID to be a core query term, both cases boil down to a query that holds only the ID of the item. The obvious idea, canonicalizing the XML query and inserting it into the URI query part, fails: with the URI encoding rules any remotely complex query would blow past URI length limits. So the RFC provides a simplified query syntax that is a subset of what the XML can say.

The abstract adds a warning: some components look like those in other URI schemes but do not act like them. The go scheme has more in common with the location-independent news scheme than any other.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing a whole question on a postcard takes too much room. So the go link is a short note that carries just the important parts of the question.

sections.title: Syntax of a go: URI
sections.content:
A CNRP URI comes in two forms. Form 1 talks to a specific server: go://[server]?common-name;attribute=[type,]value. Form 2 expresses a query meant to be sent to several different CNRP services: go:common-name;attribute=[type,]value. These two patterns are only for teaching; the ABNF grammar in Section 3.2 is the only authoritative definition.

In the grammar, cnrp-uri is go: followed by form 1 or form 2. Form 1 is //, an optional server, and an optional ? part that holds either a common name followed by any number of attribute pairs, or an ID request written id=value. Each attribute pair is ;attribute=[type,]value. The server and the unreserved characters are taken from RFC 2396.
sections.plainLanguage: A go link has an optional address of who to ask, the name you are looking for, and optional extra clues like 'only in this place'.

sections.title: Special Cases and Default Values
sections.content:
If the URI contains only the server part, it identifies a given CNRP server, not any particular query. A client can assume that such a server will at least answer the servicequery request.

If the server element is empty, its value MUST be assumed to be localhost.

CNRP's well-known HTTP transport port is 1096. If the port is not given in the server part, port 1096 SHOULD be used when the client has no prior knowledge of other ports or transports the service may support.
sections.plainLanguage: If you leave out who to ask, it means 'ask the computer right here'. If you leave out the door number, knock on door 1096.

sections.title: Encoding Rules and Transport Independence
sections.content:
The common name, query parameters and parameter values must be encoded as UTF-8. Any octet that is not one of the characters the grammar permits MUST be written as % followed by two hexadecimal characters giving the value of that octet.

CNRP can be carried over multiple transports, with HTTP mandatory to implement. When a client tries to resolve a go: URI and knows nothing about the service it names, it SHOULD use HTTP on the CNRP default port, 1096.
sections.plainLanguage: Odd letters are written as a percent sign and two digits, like a secret code that any computer can read. If you do not know how a server likes to talk, use the standard way.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives five examples. go:Mercedes%20Benz is a general query for a common name; the client packages it with its own defaults and sends it to the services it has configured. go://?Mercedes%20Benz sends the same query to the server on localhost.

go://cnrp.foo.com?Mercedes%20Benz;geography=US-ga adds a geographic attribute and targets the server at cnrp.foo.com. go://cnrp.foo.org?Martin%20J.%20D%C3%BCrst shows a UTF-8 character written with hex escaping. go://cnrp.foo.com?id=5432345 gives only an ID, so it points directly at one common-name record on one server, the sort of thing found in a link on a web page.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples show links that look up a car brand, one with a place filter, one with a letter that has two dots, and one that jumps straight to a numbered record.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond the security considerations of CNRP itself (see RFC 3367), the RFC points out a specific trap. A URI that holds only an ID, without the common name, can lead to a different site than the one a user expects.

A user may believe the link shows whatever is currently mapped to the common name "BMW", but since the name is not in the URI, a go: URI can be used without anyone knowing which common name it refers to.
sections.plainLanguage: If a link only has a secret number and no name, you cannot tell where it goes just by reading it.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content:
The IANA is asked to register the URL scheme using the template in Appendix A, following RFC 2717. The template names the scheme go, points to Section 3.2 for syntax and Section 3.4 for character encoding, and gives CNRP as the protocol that uses it.

It lists the CNRP Working Group as contact and the IESG as author and change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of link starting words needs to add 'go', so nobody else uses it for something different.
